claim: In human olfaction, plasticity is generally assumed to occur at the level of cortical synthetic processing that shares information from both nostrils.
source: In human olfaction, such plasticity is generally assumed to occur at the level of cortical synthetic processing that shares information from both nostrils.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field as stated in the abstract, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: Training-induced perceptual gain in chiral discrimination was restricted to the trained nostril.
source: Results showed that training-induced perceptual gain was restricted to the trained nostril yet partially generalized to untrained odor enantiomers in a structure- rather than quality- based manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript, supported by experimental data from both Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Training-induced perceptual gain partially generalized to untrained odor enantiomers in a structure-based manner.
source: Results showed that training-induced perceptual gain was restricted to the trained nostril yet partially generalized to untrained odor enantiomers in a structure- rather than quality- based manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2, supported by experimental data showing generalization from carvone to limonene and vice versa.

claim: Learning enhanced the differentiation of chirality (molecular configuration) as opposed to overall odor quality (odor object) per se.
source: In other words, learning enhanced the differentiation of chirality (molecular configuration) as opposed to overall odor quality (odor object) per se.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the structure-based generalization pattern observed in Experiment 2.

claim: One nostril does not readily know what the other learns in olfactory discrimination training.
source: These findings argue that, unlike earlier beliefs, one nostril does not readily know what the other learns.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the nostril-specific learning effects observed in both experiments.

claim: The initial analytical processing of the structural features of uninarial olfactory input remains plastic in human adults.
source: Moreover, the initial analytical processing of the structural features of uninarial olfactory input remains plastic in human adults.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the nostril-specific and structure-based nature of the learning observed.

claim: Different enantiomers of a chiral molecule have almost identical physical and chemical properties.
source: Whereas the different enantiomers of a chiral molecule have almost identical physical and chemical properties, they usually have different biological properties and can smell differently to the human nose (Friedman and Miller, 1971; Russell and Hills, 1971).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Different enantiomers of a chiral molecule usually have different biological properties and can smell differently to the human nose.
source: Whereas the different enantiomers of a chiral molecule have almost identical physical and chemical properties, they usually have different biological properties and can smell differently to the human nose (Friedman and Miller, 1971; Russell and Hills, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Olfactory receptors are proteins that use only one enantiomeric form (the L form) of the amino-acid building blocks.
source: After all, olfactory receptors are proteins that use only one enantiomeric form (the L form) of the amino-acid building blocks (Mombaerts, 1999).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The olfactory ability of chiral discrimination has genetic basis.
source: The olfactory ability of chiral discrimination has genetic basis (Polak et al., 1989; Saito et al., 2009) but can also be acquired through learning by human adults (Li et al., 2008), which highlights the plasticity of the adult olfactory system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The olfactory ability of chiral discrimination can be acquired through learning by human adults.
source: The olfactory ability of chiral discrimination has genetic basis (Polak et al., 1989; Saito et al., 2009) but can also be acquired through learning by human adults (Li et al., 2008), which highlights the plasticity of the adult olfactory system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The specificity of perceptual learning has long provided important clues to the locus of cortical plasticity in vision.
source: In vision, the specificity of perceptual learning has long provided important clues to the locus of cortical plasticity (Gilbert, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge in visual neuroscience cited from previous literature.

claim: Learning of texture discrimination is specific for retinal input with little interocular transfer.
source: For instance, learning of texture discrimination is specific for retinal input with little interocular transfer (Karni and Sagi, 1991), and is subserved by dynamic changes of activities in a subregion of the primary visual cortex (V1) corresponding to the trained visual field quadrant (Yotsumoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in visual learning.

claim: Learning of texture discrimination is subserved by dynamic changes of activities in a subregion of the primary visual cortex (V1) corresponding to the trained visual field quadrant.
source: For instance, learning of texture discrimination is specific for retinal input with little interocular transfer (Karni and Sagi, 1991), and is subserved by dynamic changes of activities in a subregion of the primary visual cortex (V1) corresponding to the trained visual field quadrant (Yotsumoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in visual neuroscience.

claim: The specificity of perceptual learning in olfaction has not been systematically characterized.
source: In olfaction, an ancient sense that resides in the allocortex, the specificity of perceptual learning has not been systematically characterized.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Repeatedly exposing one nostril to androstenone improved the androstenone-detection accuracy in both the exposed nostril and the unexposed nostril to the same extent in individuals who could not initially smell androstenone.
source: An earlier study tested individuals who could not smell androstenone and found that repeatedly exposing one nostril of these individuals to androstenone improved the androstenone-detection accuracy in both the exposed nostril and the unexposed nostril to the same extent (Mainland et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from previous research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The consensus is that olfactory learning takes place at the level of cortical synthetic processing that shares information from both nostrils, rather than initial analytical processing of chemical features.
source: The consensus seems to be that olfactory learning takes place at the level of cortical synthetic processing that shares information from both nostrils, rather than initial analytical processing of chemical features (Mainland et al., 2002; Wilson and Stevenson, 2003).
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field as supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The discrimination of odor enantiomers ultimately draws upon the enantioselectivity of olfactory receptors.
source: Unlike the detection of androstenone, which could involve perceptual criterion (Bremner et al., 2003), the discrimination of odor enantiomers ultimately draws upon the enantioselectivity of olfactory receptors.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the biological properties of olfactory receptors and their interaction with chiral molecules.

claim: At baseline (pretest) in Experiment 1, discrimination accuracies were at chance level (overall accuracy = 0.37 vs. chance = 0.33; t11 = 1.77, p = 0.10; binomial test, p > 0.3).
source: At baseline (pretest), discrimination accuracies were at chance (overall accuracy = 0.37 vs. chance = 0.33; t11 = 1.77, p = 0.10; binomial test, p > 0.3) irrespective of the enantiomer pair presented (α-pinene vs. 2-butanol, t11 = 1.07, p = 0.31) or the nostril of presentation (left vs. right, t11 = −0.64, p = 0.54).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Training in Experiment 1 lasted 12.1 days on average.
source: Training lasted 12.1 days on average, during which period the participants' discrimination accuracies showed a continuous improvement from chance level (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: During training in Experiment 1, participants' discrimination accuracies showed a continuous improvement from chance level.
source: Training lasted 12.1 days on average, during which period the participants' discrimination accuracies showed a continuous improvement from chance level (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Training doubled the chiral discrimination accuracy for the training pair of enantiomers presented to the trained nostril (from 0.36 to 0.70, t11 = 6.37, p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.84) in Experiment 1.
source: A direct comparison of the participants' performances at pretest and posttest (Figure 1d) showed that training doubled the chiral discrimination accuracy for the training pair of enantiomers presented to the trained nostril (from 0.36 to 0.70, t11 = 6.37, p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.84), but failed to affect the discrimination accuracy for the training pair presented to the untrained nostril (t11 = 0.52, p = 0.61), or the control pair presented to the trained (t11 = 0.60, p = 0.56) or untrained nostril (t11 = 0.84, p = 0.42).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1 supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: Training in Experiment 1 failed to affect the discrimination accuracy for the training pair presented to the untrained nostril.
source: A direct comparison of the participants' performances at pretest and posttest (Figure 1d) showed that training doubled the chiral discrimination accuracy for the training pair of enantiomers presented to the trained nostril (from 0.36 to 0.70, t11 = 6.37, p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.84), but failed to affect the discrimination accuracy for the training pair presented to the untrained nostril (t11 = 0.52, p = 0.61), or the control pair presented to the trained (t11 = 0.60, p = 0.56) or untrained nostril (t11 = 0.84, p = 0.42).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1 supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: Training in Experiment 1 failed to affect the discrimination accuracy for the control pair presented to the trained or untrained nostril.
source: A direct comparison of the participants' performances at pretest and posttest (Figure 1d) showed that training doubled the chiral discrimination accuracy for the training pair of enantiomers presented to the trained nostril (from 0.36 to 0.70, t11 = 6.37, p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.84), but failed to affect the discrimination accuracy for the training pair presented to the untrained nostril (t11 = 0.52, p = 0.61), or the control pair presented to the trained (t11 = 0.60, p = 0.56) or untrained nostril (t11 = 0.84, p = 0.42).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1 supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: Several participants noted at posttest in Experiment 1 that the trained enantiomers smelled much weaker when presented to the trained as opposed to the untrained nostril.
source: Meanwhile, several participants noted at posttest that the trained enantiomers smelled much weaker when presented to the trained as opposed to the untrained nostril.

claim: The results of Experiment 1 presented a sharp contrast to the internarial transfer of learning of androstenone detection.
source: These results presented a sharp contrast to the internarial transfer of learning of androstenone detection (Mainland et al., 2002), and pointed to plastic changes at a level in the olfactory system where uninarial information is still retained.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the current findings to previous research.

claim: The results of Experiment 1 pointed to plastic changes at a level in the olfactory system where uninarial information is still retained.

claim: Olfactory perception begins with systematic mappings of chemical structural features.
source: Considering that olfactory perception begins with systematic mappings of chemical structural features (Khan et al., 2008) yet relies heavily on memory (Wilson and Stevenson, 2003), a natural question that followed was whether such plasticity reflected enhanced differentiation of chirality (molecular configuration) or enhanced differentiation of overall odor quality (odor object) per se (Rabin, 1988) with respect to the trained enantiomers.
evidence: This is established knowledge in olfactory neuroscience cited from previous literature.

claim: Olfactory perception relies heavily on memory.
source: Considering that olfactory perception begins with systematic mappings of chemical structural features (Khan et al., 2008) yet relies heavily on memory (Wilson and Stevenson, 2003), a natural question that followed was whether such plasticity reflected enhanced differentiation of chirality (molecular configuration) or enhanced differentiation of overall odor quality (odor object) per se (Rabin, 1988) with respect to the trained enantiomers.
evidence: This is established knowledge in olfactory neuroscience cited from previous literature.

claim: Carvone and limonene enantiomers share an isopropenyl group at the chiral center and a methyl group at the para-position, and differ only by a carbonyl group.
source: They share an isopropenyl group at the chiral center and a methyl group at the para-position, that is, at the opposite side of the ring structure relative to the chiral carbon atom bearing the isopropenyl group, and differ only by a carbonyl group.
evidence: This is a description of the chemical structures shown in Figure 2a.

source: Carvone, limonene and α-pinene are all found naturally in plants yet smell quite different from one another.

claim: Participants rated the racemic mixtures of carvone, limonene and α-pinene as smelling distinctively different from one another (mean similarity rating <20 for any two of the three compounds, on a 100-unit visual analogue scale with 100 denoting extremely similar).
source: It was also unlikely that overall perceptual quality contributed to the observed generalization, as the participants rated the racemic mixtures of carvone, limonene and α-pinene as smelling distinctively different from one another (mean similarity rating <20 for any two of the three compounds, on a 100-unit visual analogue scale with 100 denoting extremely similar) and distinguished them with ceiling-level accuracy (>0.9 for any two of them vs. chance = 0.33, triangular binarial odor discrimination test).
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2 supported by experimental data.

claim: Inputs from the two nostrils remain largely separated up to the primary olfactory cortex including the piriform cortex.
source: In the olfactory system, inputs from the two nostrils remain largely separated up to the primary olfactory cortex including the piriform cortex, the largest recipient of bulbar projections that is heavily implicated in odor object perception (Carmichael et al., 1994; de Olmos et al., 1978; Gottfried, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in olfactory neuroscience cited from previous literature.

claim: The piriform cortex is the largest recipient of bulbar projections and is heavily implicated in odor object perception.

claim: Neurons in the piriform cortex exhibit no correspondence between chemical receptive field and position.
source: But in contrast to the chemotopy seen in the olfactory bulb (Khan et al., 2008; but see Soucy et al., 2009), neurons in the piriform cortex exhibit no correspondence between chemical receptive field and position, show minimal cross-habituation between odorants differing by as few as two carbons, and have been proposed to code synthetic odorant identity and odor quality (Kadohisa and Wilson, 2006; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Wilson, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge in olfactory neuroscience cited from previous literature.

claim: Experience-dependent modulations of olfactory receptor expressions in the epithelium could be utilized by downstream regions like the posterior piriform to facilitate perceptual discrimination between odor enantiomers.

claim: Only a subset of mitral-tufted cells are interconnected and the connections are weak.
source: However, as only a subset of mitral-tufted cells are interconnected and the connections are weak (Grobman et al., 2018), the activities of the mirror-symmetric mitral-tufted cells, if any, are likely insufficient to enable discrimination between the trained enantiomers presented to the untrained nostril, resulting in the observed nostril-specific gain in chiral discrimination.

claim: The results seem more consistent with the reverse hierarchy theory.
source: As such, our results seem more consistent with the reverse hierarchy theory (Ahissar and Hochstein, 2004), which asserts that learning is a gradual top-down-guided (e.g., feedback about the correct choice) increase in usability of first high- then lower-level task-relevant information and that this process is subserved by a cascade of top-to-bottom level modifications that enhance task-relevant information (e.g., configurations of the substituents attached to the chiral center).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of a theoretical framework from previous literature.

source: Supposing that learning proceeds as a countercurrent along the olfactory processing hierarchy, the detection of androstenone could be achieved by heightened attention or sensitization to its olfactory quality (amplification of a weak signal which lowers detection threshold) and hence possibly engages a higher generalizing level, whereas the learning of chiral discrimination likely relies more on lower-level inputs and is thus more specific.
